findings.desc: getClientsWithPermission uses resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...). However, admin-permission V2 resources are created via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource -> ResourceStore.create(...), which never calls resource.setType(...). Unlike V1 ClientPermissions (which explicitly does resource.setType("Client")), the V2 resources have a null type, so findByType("Clients") matches nothing and this method always returns an empty set. This silently breaks AvailableRoleMappingResource.getRoleIdsWithPermission for FGAP V2 (clients with MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE permission are dropped). Additionally, even if type matched, the per-type "all-clients" resource has name "Clients" (not a client id), and the method adds resource.getName() to the result; the caller then calls realm.getClientById(cid), which would NPE for the "Clients" entry. Consider setting the type on creation and filtering out the resource-type resource / returning client ids consistently.
findings.title: getClientsWithPermission relies on resource type that is never set

findings.desc: The cleanup listener is now gated on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1). But management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, and V2 implementations (e.g. ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, UserPermissionsV2, etc.) throw UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). V2 depends only on AUTHORIZATION, not on V1, so both features can be enabled at once. In that configuration a ClientRemovedEvent/RoleRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent would invoke management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...) on the V2 impl and throw, breaking client/role/group deletion. The guard should also exclude the V2 case (e.g. enabled(V1) && !enabled(V2)), or V2 impls must no-op instead of throwing here.
findings.title: Removal listener may call V2 setPermissionsEnabled which throws

findings.desc: In V2 a group resource's name is the group id (see resolveGroup in AdminPermissionsSchema, and hasPermission(group.getId()) uses resourceStore.findByName). Here the loop passes groupResource.getId() (the resource's internal UUID) to hasPermission and adds it to the result set. hasPermission does findByName(server, groupId) which won't match on a UUID, so it falls through to the all-groups fallback instead of evaluating the specific group. And the returned set contains resource UUIDs rather than group ids. These ids are consumed as group ids by UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource (session attribute UserModel.GROUPS and getUsersCount(..., groupIds)), so member-scoped user visibility is broken. Use groupResource.getName() in both places.

A manage check should require the MANAGE scope only, not VIEW. (The interface javadoc documents VIEW-or-MANAGE for V2, but that itself appears to be the escalation.) Consider hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE).

findings.desc: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generatedCodes list to JSON and passes it as the challengeResponse of the UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). When a federated user storage implements CredentialInputUpdater and accepts the update, it receives the recovery codes in plaintext (the local provider stores them hashed). Recovery codes are authentication secrets; forwarding them unhashed to external storage is a security consideration worth documenting and/or reconsidering. At minimum the asymmetry (hashed locally, plaintext to storage) should be called out so external storage implementors know they must hash on their side.

findings.desc: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) BEFORE CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (or any error), the cache entry (keyed only on DeviceID) is already set. Subsequent requests from the same device hit the cache and return nil within the 29-min TTL, so authentication succeeds even though the device was never stored and is over the limit. This both defeats the new limit enforcement and makes auth inconsistent (first request rejected, later ones allowed). Set the cache entry only after a successful write (and/or evict it on error).

@@ -94,6 +92,8 @@

findings.desc: CreateOrUpdateDevice reads the count with CountDevices and then inserts in a separate statement without any locking/transaction. Under concurrent anonymous requests for distinct new devices, multiple callers can all observe count < deviceLimit and then each insert, pushing the stored device count past deviceLimit. If strict enforcement matters, perform the check and insert atomically (e.g. a single conditional INSERT ... SELECT WHERE (count) < limit, or a transaction with an appropriate lock).

findings.desc: The previous implementation tagged the device in a background goroutine with a 2m timeout and panic recovery. It is now called inline during Authenticate using the request context. This adds a DB count + insert/update to every anonymous request latency path, and removes the panic guard. A slow or unavailable DB will now delay each anonymous auth (bounded only by the request ctx) and non-limit errors are swallowed but still block. Consider keeping the limit check synchronous but the best-effort tagging/DB write off the hot path, or document the intended latency impact.

findings.desc: updateDevice treats RowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, RowsAffected counts changed rows, not matched rows (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), so updating an existing device with identical client_ip/user_agent/updated_at returns 0 and would incorrectly surface as 'device limit reached' for a device that actually exists. updated_at is set to time.Now() each call so a collision is unlikely, but a matched-but-unchanged row would be misclassified. Consider checking existence explicitly rather than relying on affected-row count.

findings.desc: permDenialCache caches negative Check results for up to shortCacheTTL (30s) and is consulted BEFORE the allow (permCache) path. Because nothing invalidates permDenialCache on permission changes (there is no explicit cache invalidation anywhere; both caches rely on TTL), a user who is granted a permission will keep getting Allowed:false for up to 30s even if permCache has already been refreshed with the new grant — the early denial-cache return short-circuits before the allow path is evaluated. findings.desc: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` do not create dynamic/catch-all keys. `ZodString.toString()` returns the literal string "[object Object]" for both, so the object schema ends up as `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() }` (the second property overwrites the first). As a result, when credential sharing is enabled, zod strips every real field (expiry_date, token_type, refresh_token, etc.) except access_token, so refreshed credentials lose their expiry and other data. Use passthrough/catchall instead, e.g. `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()`.
